newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rail strike in France has slight impact on travel.
newsitem.headline: Rail strike in France has slight impact on travel.

text.p: France's second rail strike in a week's time had little impact on the travelling public on Wednesday morning as most workers ignored a union appeal to stay away in protest against government rail reform plans.
The SNCF state railways said most high-speed TGV trains were operating normally as were as high-speed services from Paris to London and Brussels.
Also operating normally were trains heading for the Alps, where many families planned to begin ski holidays during the February school break.
The one-day rail strike called by the Communist-led CGT union, began at midnight (2300 GMT) on Tuesday and was scheduled to end at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Thursday.
A similar strike took place last Thursday, called by the CGT and the Socialist CFDT union. For this week, however, the CFDT chose to stage a protest rally rather than strike a second time.

The government has proposed setting up a state holding company which would take over the bulk of the SNCF's debts of 208 billion francs ($37.4 billion) but which would become owner of the network and charge the SNCF rail usage fees.
Most unions back rail reform but the CGT and CFDT fear the plan will lead to a break-up of the SNCF, threatening jobs and deteriorating working conditions.

France has been hit by sporadic labour unrest over the past five months due to near-record unemployment of 12.7 percent and government austerity plans aimed at helping Paris qualify for a single European currency.
Unions fighting for a shorter working week and earlier retirement at tram and urban transit companies in towns outside Paris have called for a strike on Thursday.
And seven civil service unions set a one-day strike for March 6 by millions of public employees, over a government pay offer they deemed inadequate.
The government has offered a 2.8 percent pay rise over 1997 and 1998, rejecting union calls for a bigger hike to compensate for a pay freeze imposed last year.

Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben said a "catch-up" for 1996 would have cost 20 billion francs and that the government was determined to show the financial markets and its European Union partners that France was committed to spending restraint. ($ = 5.555 French Francs)
